title: A budget, not an equal share
outcomes: Splits a 15-minute game into an opening share, a middlegame share, an endgame share and a reserve that add up to the whole
Works out how many long thinks a middlegame share allows once routine moves are paid for
Tells a routine, a critical and a forced position apart and says whether a flat share is enough
Writes a budget to try in his next game and names the clock record that will check it

steps.text: A **time budget** is a plan for where the clock goes: a share for each phase, a reserve for the end, and room to think longer on the few moves that matter. **The same time on every move is not a budget**: it pays as much for a forced reply as for a decision. Every number here is a first guess to test against your own clock.

steps.prompt: A 15+0 game gives each player 15 minutes and adds nothing. Say the reserve is 2 minutes, the opening 3 and the endgame 3. The middlegame is moves 13 to 30, which is 18 moves. Work these out before you read on.

fields.label: If each middlegame move costs a routine 10 seconds, how many one-minute thinks fit in what is left of the middlegame share?

steps.text: **Pay for routine moves first.** Give routine moves a small price and keep the rest of the phase share for critical moments, such as a tempting capture that may cost material. Forced replies cost almost nothing. The prices (10 seconds, one minute) are a rule of thumb to adjust, not a measured optimum.

steps.caption: White to move. The pawn on e4 can be taken. Is this a routine move or a critical one?

line.say: Nxe4 takes a pawn. It looks free.
Nb3+ is check, and the knight also attacks the queen on d2.
The king must move, and the queen stays attacked.
Rxd2 takes the knight back. White gave a queen for a knight and a pawn.

claims.statement: Nxe4 is rated at least five pawns worse than the best move.
Along the engine line Nxe4 ends with White five or more points down.
Qf4 is the engine's best move.

steps.title: How much of the budget does it deserve?
steps.prompt: The first position was routine: about 10 seconds was the right price. In this one, decide: is it critical, so it needs extra from the pool, or routine, so the usual price is enough? A forced move, with one legal move, gets almost nothing; you meet one in the next exercises. Predict, then check.

steps.text: **When a budget works.** It works if you check it: compare your clock at move 12, move 30 and the end with the plan after each game. It fails when rigid: on a critical move, take the minute and pay it back from the share. It barely binds with a big increment (60+30 is about 120 seconds a move over 40 moves). Treat it as a rule of thumb.

steps.prompt: Sort each case. Does a time budget work, fail, or not apply? Choose, then save to see my answer. The answers are my judgement, not a measurement.

fields.label: Every move gets 20 seconds, whatever the position.
Routine moves cost about 10 seconds, a critical move may take a minute from the phase share, and the clock is written down at move 12, move 30 and the end.
The plan says 10 seconds a move, and you play a tempting capture in 10 seconds without looking at the reply.
A 60+30 game of 40 moves, and you still have most of an hour on the clock.

steps.text: **What the app does for you now, and when it stops.** The app does not time your games, and an imported game is not read for clock times. So the budget lives on paper: write your clock at move 12, move 30 and the end of each game. A time-per-move record is planned, not built. Once you can revise a budget from your notes, you do not need this page.

steps.prompt: Write the budget you will try in your next game. The numbers must add up to your total.
